Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only astronomical object known to harbor life.[1] About 71 percent of its surface is covered by oceans of liquid water, and the rest is continents and islands.

Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago from the disc of dust and gas around the young Sun. Its single natural satellite, the Moon, keeps the tilt of its axis steady and raises the tides.

Etymology

[edit]

The English word comes from an old Germanic word for the ground and the soil. It is the only planet whose English name is not taken from Greek or Roman myth.

Physical characteristics

[edit]

Earth is the densest planet of the Solar System and the largest of the four rocky planets.[2]

Shape

[edit]

Earth is close to a sphere but flattened at the poles, so the diameter at the equator is about 43 km larger than the diameter from pole to pole.

Chemical composition

[edit]

By mass, the planet is mostly iron (about 32 percent), oxygen (30 percent), silicon (15 percent) and magnesium (14 percent), with smaller amounts of sulfur, nickel, calcium and aluminium.[3]

The crust is made up mostly of oxides: silica alone accounts for about 60 percent of it, and alumina for another 15 percent. Its rocks are composed of light minerals such as quartz and feldspar.

Internal structure

[edit]

Earth's interior is divided into layers by their chemistry and by how they flow: a thin crust, a thick rocky mantle, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core.[4]

The mantle is made of dense silicate rock rich in iron and magnesium; it is solid, but over millions of years it creeps like a very thick fluid.

The outer core is a layer of liquid iron and nickel about 2,200 km thick, and the currents in it make the planet's magnetic field.

The inner core is a solid ball of iron and nickel about 1,220 km in radius, where the temperature may reach 6,000 °C, about as hot as the surface of the Sun.

Surface

[edit]

The surface is made of a few large tectonic plates and many small ones that move a few centimetres a year. Where plates meet there are earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain ranges.

Hydrosphere

[edit]

Earth's water is mostly in the oceans; seawater is a solution of salts with about 35 grams of salt in each kilogram of water. Ice caps and glaciers hold most of the fresh water.

Atmosphere

[edit]

Earth's atmosphere consists of about 78 percent nitrogen and 21 percent oxygen by volume, with small amounts of argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour.[5]

The atmosphere has no sharp edge; it thins out with height, and three quarters of its mass lies within 11 km of the surface.

It shields life from ultraviolet light through the ozone layer and keeps the surface warm through the greenhouse effect.

Orbit and rotation

[edit]

Earth turns once on its axis in about 24 hours and goes around the Sun once in about 365.25 days. Its axis is tilted by about 23.4 degrees, which gives the seasons.

Moon

[edit]

The Moon is about a quarter of Earth's diameter. It is made largely of rock like that of Earth's mantle, which supports the idea that it formed from debris after a giant impact.

Geology

[edit]

Earth's continental crust is made mostly of granite and similar rocks, while the oceanic crust is made of basalt.

Earth's soils are a mixture of weathered rock, organic matter, water and air.

Earth's sedimentary rocks are made from layers of sand, mud and the shells of sea creatures pressed together over time.

Earth's oldest rocks, found in Canada, are about four billion years old.

Life

[edit]

Life appeared on Earth at least 3.5 billion years ago. Plants and other photosynthetic organisms produced the oxygen of the atmosphere over billions of years.

Earth's biosphere is made up of all its living things, from bacteria in deep rock to forests and whales.

Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and the second smallest planet in the Solar System. It is often called the Red Planet because iron oxide in its dust gives it a reddish colour.[6]

Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, which may be captured asteroids. Its day is only slightly longer than a day on Earth.

Physical characteristics

[edit]

Mars has about half the diameter of Earth and about a tenth of its mass. Its surface gravity is a little over a third of Earth's.

Internal structure

[edit]

Like Earth, Mars has separated into a dense metal core with lighter rock above it.

Its core is made of iron and nickel with a large share of sulfur, and it is thought to be at least partly liquid.[7]

The mantle is made of silicate rock, and the crust above it consists of basalt that came from ancient volcanoes.

Surface geology

[edit]

Mars's soil is made up of fine basaltic dust mixed with salts such as perchlorates, which are poisonous to most life.

The reddish dust is produced by weathering of iron-rich rock, and it is spread across the planet by dust storms.

Atmosphere

[edit]

The atmosphere of Mars is very thin, with a pressure at the surface less than one percent of Earth's.

It is about 95 percent carbon dioxide, 2.8 percent nitrogen and 2 percent argon, with traces of oxygen and water.[8]

Methane has been reported in it from time to time, but its source is not known.

Polar caps

[edit]

Mars has two permanent polar ice caps. They are made mostly of water ice, and in winter a layer of frozen carbon dioxide forms on top of them.

Moons

[edit]

Phobos and Deimos are small and irregular. Phobos is about 22 km across and Deimos about 12 km.

Both moons are made of dark, carbon-rich rock that resembles some asteroids.

Exploration

[edit]

More than fifty spacecraft have been sent to Mars, and about half of them reached it. Rovers have studied its rocks and found signs that liquid water once flowed there.

Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun and the second largest in the Solar System, after Jupiter. It is a gas giant, about nine times as wide as Earth.[9]

Saturn is best known for its bright system of rings, the largest of any planet.

Physical characteristics

[edit]

Saturn is so light for its size that its mean density is lower than that of water. It spins very fast and bulges at the equator.

Internal structure

[edit]

Saturn is composed mostly of hydrogen and helium, like Jupiter.[10]

Its core is thought to consist of rock and ice, surrounded by a thick layer of metallic hydrogen.

Saturn gives off more heat than it receives from the Sun, perhaps because helium droplets sink through the hydrogen.

Atmosphere

[edit]

The outer atmosphere is about 96 percent hydrogen and 3 percent helium by volume. Its clouds are made of ammonia ice crystals, with water clouds deeper down.

Winds in the upper atmosphere reach 1,800 km/h, faster than on Jupiter.

Planetary rings

[edit]

The rings extend from about 7,000 km to 80,000 km above the equator, but in most places they are only about 10 metres thick.

The particles of the rings are almost entirely water ice, with a little rocky material, and range from specks of dust to blocks the size of a house.[11]

Scientists disagree about their age; some think they formed only a few hundred million years ago.

Moons

[edit]

Saturn has more known moons than any other planet. Titan, the largest, is bigger than the planet Mercury.

Titan has a thick atmosphere that consists mainly of nitrogen, and lakes of liquid methane and ethane on its surface.

Enceladus throws out jets of water vapour and ice from an ocean under its crust.

Observation

[edit]

Saturn is the most distant planet easily seen with the naked eye. Galileo first saw the rings in 1610 but could not tell what they were.

Chocolate

Chocolate is a food made from roasted and ground cacao seeds, sold as a liquid, a paste or a solid block.[12] Cacao has been eaten in Mesoamerica for at least three thousand years.

The seeds are fermented, dried, roasted and cracked; the pieces, called nibs, are ground into a thick paste known as chocolate liquor.

Etymology

The word reached English from Spanish, which took it from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs.

History

The Olmec, Maya and Aztecs drank cacao as a bitter, spiced drink.[13] The Spanish brought it to Europe in the sixteenth century, where sugar was added.

In 1847 a British firm pressed the first solid bar, and in 1875 a Swiss maker added condensed milk to make milk chocolate.

Types

Several kinds of chocolate are sold, depending on how much cocoa solids, cocoa butter and milk they hold.

White chocolate has cocoa butter, sugar and milk solids but none of the dark cocoa solids, which is why some people say it is not chocolate at all.[14]

Milk chocolate is made with milk powder or condensed milk, and must hold at least 10 percent cocoa solids in the United States.

Dark chocolate is produced by adding fat and sugar to cocoa, with little or no milk; bittersweet bars may be more than 70 percent cocoa.

Chocolate chips are made with less cocoa butter so that they keep their shape in an oven.

Compound chocolate is a blend of cocoa with vegetable fats instead of cocoa butter, and it is cheaper to make.

Production

Chocolate liquor is produced by grinding the roasted nibs, and it can be pressed to separate cocoa butter from cocoa powder.

Modern chocolate is a mixture of chocolate liquor, extra cocoa butter, sugar and often an emulsifier such as soy lecithin.

Conching, a long stirring of the warm mass, smooths its texture and removes some sour flavours.

Tempering, which heats and cools the chocolate in turn, gives the snap and shine of a good bar.

Health effects

Chocolate contains moderate amounts of caffeine and theobromine, which are poisonous to dogs and cats in large doses.[15]

Its fat and sugar make it high in energy; a 100-gram bar of milk chocolate holds over 500 kilocalories.

Culinary uses

Chocolate is used in cakes, biscuits, ice cream, sauces and drinks, and in some savoury dishes such as the mole sauces of Mexico.

Hot chocolate is made with melted chocolate or cocoa powder whisked into hot milk.

Ganache is an emulsion of chocolate and cream, used to fill and cover cakes and truffles.

Chocolate truffles are made of ganache rolled into balls and coated with cocoa powder or tempered chocolate.

Cocoa powder is produced by pressing most of the fat out of chocolate liquor and grinding the cake that remains.

Dutch-process cocoa is treated with an alkali, which makes it darker and milder.

Chocolate spreads are a blend of sugar, vegetable oil, cocoa and often hazelnuts.

Couverture is a chocolate made with extra cocoa butter, which melts thin for coating.

Storage

Chocolate keeps best at 15 to 17 °C away from strong smells. A grey film on old chocolate, called bloom, is fat or sugar that has risen to the surface; it is safe to eat.

Economics

Ivory Coast and Ghana grow about 60 percent of the world's cocoa.

Chocolate is a mixture of ingredients bought on world markets, so its price follows the prices of cocoa and sugar.

Labor

Much of the world's cocoa is grown on small farms in West Africa, where child labor has been reported on many of them.

Steel

Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon, with up to about two percent carbon by weight, that is stronger and tougher than iron alone.[16]

Because of its strength and low cost, steel is used for buildings, bridges, ships, cars, machines, tools and weapons. World production is close to two billion tonnes a year.

Material properties

[edit]

Iron atoms in steel are arranged in crystals; carbon atoms sit between them and stop the layers of iron from sliding, which makes the metal harder.

Too much carbon makes the steel brittle, so most structural steel holds well under one percent.

Types

[edit]

Carbon steel

[edit]

Carbon steel is plain iron and carbon with only small traces of other elements, and it is by far the most common kind.

Mild steel, with about 0.2 percent carbon, is easy to weld and bend.

Stainless steel

[edit]

Stainless steel holds at least 11 percent chromium, often with nickel, and the chromium forms a thin film of oxide that keeps it from rusting.[17]

The common kitchen grade, called 18/8, has 18 percent chromium and 8 percent nickel.

Tool steel

[edit]

Tool steels are made with tungsten, molybdenum or vanadium, which keep them hard when they get hot in cutting.

Production

[edit]

Most steel is produced by blowing oxygen through molten pig iron, which burns off the extra carbon.

Pig iron itself is made by heating iron ore with coke and limestone in a blast furnace.

About a third of new steel is made from scrap, melted in electric arc furnaces.

Steel is recycled more than any other material, and it can be melted again without losing its qualities.

Heat treatment

[edit]

Steel is hardened by heating it until it glows and then quenching it in water or oil; it is then tempered by reheating to a lower temperature, which makes it less brittle.

Case-hardened steel is produced by heating low-carbon steel in a carbon-rich atmosphere so that only its surface becomes hard.

Coatings

[edit]

Galvanized steel is made by dipping steel in molten zinc, which protects it from rust even where it is scratched.

Tinplate is steel coated with a thin layer of tin, used for food cans.

Weathering steel is formulated with copper and chromium so that its rust forms a tight protective layer.

Uses

[edit]

Reinforcing bars are made from recycled steel and cast into concrete.

Steel cables for bridges consist of thousands of thin wires twisted together.

Car bodies are produced by pressing thin steel sheet in large dies.

Steel wool is made of fine steel filaments and is used for cleaning and polishing.

History

[edit]

Steel was known in antiquity, but it was costly until 1856, when Henry Bessemer found a cheap way to make it in bulk.

Crucible steel from southern India, called wootz, was prized in the Middle East for swords.

Damascus steel blades were made from wootz ingots and show a wavy pattern.

Bronze

Bronze is an alloy consisting mostly of copper, commonly with about 12 percent tin and often with small amounts of other metals such as aluminium, manganese or zinc.[18]

Bronze was the first alloy made in quantity, and it gave its name to the Bronze Age, when it was used for tools, weapons and armour.

History

[edit]

The earliest bronzes were made with arsenic rather than tin, perhaps by accident, from ores that held both metals.

Tin bronze appeared in the Near East before 3000 BC, and tin was carried long distances because it is rare.

Composition

[edit]

Modern standard bronze is 88 percent copper and 12 percent tin.

Bell metal has more tin, about 20 to 25 percent, which makes it hard and makes it ring.

Aluminium bronze holds 5 to 11 percent aluminium and resists corrosion in seawater, so it is used for ship propellers.

Phosphor bronze is made with a small amount of phosphorus, and it is used for springs and for the strings of guitars.

Properties

[edit]

Bronze is harder than copper and melts at a lower temperature, about 950 °C, which made it easy to cast.

It does not spark when struck against a hard surface, so bronze tools are used near flammable materials.

Uses

[edit]

Bronze statues are made by the lost-wax method: a wax model is covered with clay, the wax is melted out and molten bronze is poured into the space.

Cymbals and bells are cast from bronze because of its sound.

Bronze medals are given for third place in many sports.

Bronze bearings are made with a little lead, which makes them slide easily.

Bronze ship fittings are produced by casting in sand moulds.

Coins called bronze are often made of copper with only a little tin and zinc.

Bronze wool is made of fine bronze threads and does not rust like steel wool.

Bronze sculptures consist of a thin shell of metal around a hollow core.

pages.wikipedia_en_all_maxi_2026-01/Cement:
Cement

A cement is a binder, a substance that sets and hardens and binds other materials together.[19] Cement is seldom used on its own; it is used to bind sand and gravel together.

Cement mixed with fine aggregate makes mortar for masonry, and with sand and gravel it makes concrete, the most widely used man-made material.

Chemistry

Portland cement is produced by heating limestone and clay to about 1,450 °C in a kiln, which forms hard lumps called clinker.

The clinker is ground to a fine powder with a little gypsum, which slows the setting.

When water is added, the calcium silicates in it react to form crystals that lock the mixture together.

Mortar

Mortar is a paste of cement, sand and water used to bond bricks and stones. A common mix for brickwork is one part cement to five or six parts sand.

Lime is often added to mortar to make it easier to spread and slightly flexible.

Concrete

Concrete is a mixture of cement, water, sand and gravel or crushed stone.[20] A typical mix is about one part cement, two parts sand and three parts gravel by volume.

Concrete is strong when squeezed but weak when pulled, so steel bars are cast into it to make reinforced concrete.

History

The Romans made a strong cement from lime and volcanic ash, and some of their harbours still stand.

Portland cement was patented in 1824 by Joseph Aspdin, who named it after the stone of the Isle of Portland.

Environmental impact

Cement production gives off about eight percent of the world's carbon dioxide, both from burning fuel and from the limestone itself.

Workers breathing cement dust over many years can suffer lung disease, and wet cement can burn skin.

Safety

Wet cement is strongly alkaline and can cause chemical burns; gloves and eye protection should be worn, and skin that touches it should be washed with water at once.

Glass

Glass is a hard, brittle and usually transparent solid that has no crystal structure, so its atoms are arranged at random like those of a liquid.[21]

The most common glass, soda-lime glass, is used for windows, bottles and jars, and it is made from sand, soda ash and limestone.

Composition

[edit]

Soda-lime glass is about 70 percent silica, with sodium oxide that lowers the melting point and calcium oxide that keeps the glass from dissolving in water.

Borosilicate glass contains boron trioxide, which makes it resist sudden heat, so it is used for laboratory flasks and oven dishes.

Lead glass, sold as crystal, has a large share of lead oxide, which makes it sparkle and gives it weight.

Fused quartz is nearly pure silica; it is made by melting quartz sand at a very high temperature.

Manufacture

[edit]

Window glass is made by floating molten glass on a bath of liquid tin, which gives a flat, smooth sheet.

Bottles are blown into moulds by machines that make thousands of them an hour.

Natural glass

[edit]

Obsidian is a natural glass produced by the rapid cooling of lava. It was used for sharp blades in the Stone Age.

History

[edit]

The oldest glass objects, beads from Mesopotamia, date to about 2500 BC.

Glassblowing was invented on the eastern Mediterranean coast in the first century BC.

Recycling

[edit]

Glass can be melted and made into new glass again and again; using broken glass, called cullet, saves energy in the furnace.

Kinds of glass products

[edit]

Safety glass for car windscreens is made of two sheets of glass with a layer of plastic between them, so that it cracks without falling apart.

Toughened glass is produced by heating a finished sheet and cooling its surfaces quickly with jets of air.

Glass wool, used to insulate houses, is made from glass melted and spun into fine fibres.

Optical fibres are made of extremely pure glass drawn into threads thinner than a hair.

Coloured glass is made by adding small amounts of metal oxides: cobalt for blue, chromium for green, gold for red.

Mirrors are made by coating the back of a sheet of glass with a thin layer of silver or aluminium.

Glass bricks consist of two pressed halves sealed together around an air space.

pages.wikipedia_en_all_maxi_2026-01/Bread:
Bread

Bread is a staple food prepared from a dough of flour, usually wheat, and water, usually by baking.[22] It has been made for at least ten thousand years.

Most breads are leavened, made to rise by yeast or by a sourdough culture, but flatbreads are not.

Types

[edit]

Sourdough bread is made with a starter of wild yeasts and lactic acid bacteria, which gives it a sour taste.

Rye bread is made from rye flour, often mixed with wheat flour, and it is dense and dark.

Soda bread is raised with baking soda and buttermilk instead of yeast.

Chapati and tortillas are flatbreads; a chapati is just whole-wheat flour, water and a pinch of salt.

Ingredients

[edit]

The basic loaf needs only four things: flour, water, salt and yeast.

Wheat flour holds the proteins that form gluten, an elastic web that traps the gas from the yeast.

Fat, sugar, milk or eggs may be added to make the bread softer or richer.

Preparation

[edit]

The dough is kneaded to develop the gluten, left to rise, shaped, left to rise again and baked.

A loaf is baked when it sounds hollow when tapped underneath, at about 96 °C inside.

History

[edit]

Charred crumbs of flatbread about 14,000 years old have been found in Jordan.

In ancient Egypt bread was made from emmer wheat and was a large part of the wages of workers.

Nutrition

[edit]

White bread is made from flour that has had the bran and germ removed, so it holds less fibre than wholemeal bread.

pages.wikipedia_en_all_maxi_2026-01/Soap:
Soap

Soap is a salt of a fatty acid, used for washing, bathing and cleaning.[23] Its molecules have one end that holds on to water and one that holds on to oil, so it carries grease away in water.

Soap is made by mixing fats or oils with a strong alkali such as lye in a reaction called saponification.

Ingredients

[edit]

Hard bar soap uses sodium hydroxide, while soft and liquid soaps use potassium hydroxide.

The fats can come from animals, such as tallow, or from plants, such as olive, coconut and palm oil.

Glycerol is formed in the same reaction; many makers leave it in, which makes the soap gentler on skin.

Making soap

[edit]

In the cold process, lye dissolved in water is stirred into melted fat at about 40 °C until it thickens, and the bars then cure for four to six weeks.

Lye is caustic and can blind; soap makers wear goggles and gloves and always add the lye to the water, never the water to the lye.

Castile soap is made from olive oil and takes its name from a region of Spain.

Effect on germs

[edit]

Washing hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds removes many germs; the soap breaks the fatty coat of some viruses.[24]

History

[edit]

A recipe for soap from fats and wood ashes was written in Babylon about 2800 BC.

Egg as food

Humans and their ancestors have eaten eggs for millions of years. The eggs of chickens are by far the most eaten, followed by those of ducks, quail and geese.[25]

An egg has a hard shell, a clear white called albumen, and a yellow yolk in the middle. Eggs are a cheap source of protein and are used in cooking all over the world.

Anatomy

[edit]

The eggshell is about 95 percent calcium carbonate, laid down as tiny crystals, with a little protein holding them together.[26]

The shell has thousands of tiny pores that let air and moisture pass, which is why an old egg floats.

Two thin membranes lie under the shell, and at the wide end they separate to form an air cell.

The egg white is about 90 percent water; the rest is mostly proteins, chief among them ovalbumin.

The yolk holds nearly all the fat of the egg, together with most of its vitamins and iron, and its colour depends on what the hen eats.

Twisted cords called chalazae hold the yolk in the centre of the white.

Nutrition

[edit]

A large chicken egg weighs about 50 grams without the shell and supplies about 70 kilocalories and 6 grams of protein.

Eggs hold vitamin B12, riboflavin, vitamin D and choline, but little vitamin C.

One yolk holds about 185 milligrams of cholesterol.

Culinary uses

[edit]

Eggs can be boiled, fried, poached, scrambled or baked, and they bind, raise and thicken many other foods.

Mayonnaise is an emulsion of oil and egg yolk with vinegar or lemon juice, and the yolk's lecithin keeps the oil from separating.

Meringue is made with egg whites beaten with sugar until they hold stiff peaks.

Custard is a mixture of milk or cream with egg yolks, cooked gently until it thickens.

Omelettes are made of beaten eggs cooked quickly in a pan and folded around a filling.

Egg wash, made of beaten egg with a little water or milk, gives pastry a shiny brown crust.

Cakes made with whole eggs rise because the beaten egg traps air.

Pasta dough in northern Italy is made with flour and egg yolks rather than water.

Hollandaise sauce is an emulsion of butter and egg yolks with lemon juice, kept warm over hot water.

Egg noodles are made from wheat flour mixed with whole eggs, which gives them their yellow colour.

Eggnog is a mixture of milk, cream, sugar and beaten eggs, often with rum or brandy.

Royal icing is made of egg whites and icing sugar, and it sets hard on cakes and biscuits.

Egg fried rice is made with cooked rice, scrambled egg and vegetables fried together.

Preserved eggs

[edit]

Century eggs are made by coating duck eggs in a mixture of clay, ash, salt and quicklime for several weeks.

Pickled eggs are hard-boiled eggs kept in vinegar or brine.

Powdered egg is produced by spray-drying beaten egg, and it keeps for years.

Food safety

[edit]

Raw and undercooked eggs can carry Salmonella bacteria, which cause food poisoning.[27]

Cooking eggs until both the white and the yolk are firm kills the bacteria; dishes with eggs should reach 71 °C (160 °F).

Eggs should be kept cold, and cracked or dirty eggs should not be used.

Washing eggs removes a natural coating, so in many countries eggs sold in shops are not washed and need not be refrigerated.

Production

[edit]

China produces more eggs than any other country, about a third of the world's total.

A modern laying hen lays about 300 eggs a year.

Tooth

For teeth of humans, see Human tooth.

A tooth is a hard, calcified structure found in the jaws of many vertebrates and used to break down food.[28] Some animals, such as many fish, also use them for defence.

Teeth are not made of bone; they are built of tissues of different density and hardness that grow from the outer layer of the embryo and the tissue beneath it.

Structure

[edit]

A tooth has a crown above the gum and one or more roots set in the jawbone.

Enamel, the outer layer of the crown, is the hardest substance in the human body. It is about 96 percent mineral, mostly hydroxyapatite, a crystalline calcium phosphate, and it holds no living cells.[29]

Dentin, under the enamel, is about 70 percent mineral and is softer and yellower than enamel.

Cementum covers the root and anchors the fibres of the ligament that holds the tooth in its socket.

The pulp in the centre is soft tissue made up of blood vessels, nerves and connective tissue.

Teeth are composed of the same minerals as bone, but they cannot heal themselves in the same way.

Development

[edit]

Humans grow two sets of teeth: twenty milk teeth, which begin to come in at about six months, and thirty-two permanent teeth.

The last molars, often called wisdom teeth, come in between the ages of 17 and 25, if at all.

Teeth of other animals

[edit]

Shark teeth are made of a tissue like dentin covered with a hard layer; a shark may lose thousands of teeth in its life.

The tusks of elephants are long incisors made of dentin, the material sold as ivory.

Rodents have incisors that never stop growing and are worn down by gnawing.

Snakes' fangs are hollow or grooved teeth that carry venom.

Decay and care

[edit]

Tooth decay happens when bacteria in plaque turn sugars into acid, which dissolves the enamel.[30]

Fluoride makes enamel harder to dissolve, and it is added to toothpaste and, in many places, to drinking water.

Brushing twice a day with a fluoride toothpaste, and eating less sugar, prevents most decay.

Toothpaste is made with a mild abrasive, a fluoride compound, a detergent and flavouring.

Fossil record

[edit]

Teeth survive far better than bone, so many extinct animals are known only from their teeth.

Comet

A comet is an icy, small body of the Solar System that warms and begins to release gases when it passes close to the Sun.[31] This makes a thin, fuzzy atmosphere around it, the coma, and often a tail.

Comets have orbits that are usually long ellipses; some return within a few years, others only after thousands of years.

Physical characteristics

Nucleus

The solid core of a comet, the nucleus, is a loose mass of rock, dust, water ice and frozen gases such as carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, methane and ammonia.[32]

This picture of a comet as a dirty snowball was put forward by Fred Whipple in 1950.

Most nuclei are a few kilometres across and are among the darkest objects in the Solar System, reflecting only about four percent of the light that falls on them.

Coma

The coma is made of gas and dust that boil off the nucleus; it can be wider than the Sun.

The coma is mostly water vapour, with some carbon dioxide and other gases.

Tails

Comets often have two tails, and both always point away from the Sun.

The dust tail is made of tiny grains pushed out by sunlight; it is curved and yellowish.

The ion tail is composed of charged gas carried by the solar wind, and it is straight and blue.

Tails can be over 150 million kilometres long.

Orbits

Short-period comets come back in less than 200 years and are thought to come from the Kuiper belt beyond Neptune.

Long-period comets fall in from the far Oort cloud, a vast shell of icy bodies around the Solar System.

Notable comets

Halley's Comet returns about every 76 years and was last seen from Earth in 1986.

Comet Hale–Bopp was visible to the naked eye for a record 18 months in 1996 and 1997.

Meteor showers

When Earth passes through the trail of dust left by a comet, the grains burn up in the air as a meteor shower; the Perseids each August come from Comet Swift–Tuttle.

Sun

Sun

Equatorial radius696,000 km
Mass1.989 × 10^30 kg
Surface temperature5,772 K
Age4.6 billion years

The Sun is the star at the centre of the Solar System. It is a massive, nearly perfect sphere of hot plasma, heated by nuclear fusion in its core.[33]

The Sun is by far the most important source of energy for life on Earth. Its light takes about eight minutes and twenty seconds to reach us.

Composition

[edit]

By mass the Sun is about 73 percent hydrogen and 25 percent helium, with small amounts of heavier elements such as oxygen, carbon, neon and iron.[34]

The heavier elements are called metals by astronomers, even those that are not metals in chemistry.

Structure

[edit]

Core

[edit]

The core reaches out to about a quarter of the Sun's radius and has a temperature of about 15 million kelvin.

In the core, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium, and by now the core is about 60 percent helium by mass.

Every second, the fusion turns about four million tonnes of matter into energy.

Radiative zone

[edit]

Above the core, energy moves outward as light that is absorbed and given off again by the plasma, a journey that can take a hundred thousand years.

Convective zone

[edit]

In the outer third, hot plasma rises and cooler plasma sinks, like water boiling in a pot.

Photosphere

[edit]

The photosphere is the visible surface, at about 5,800 kelvin. Darker, cooler spots on it, called sunspots, come and go in a cycle of about eleven years.

Corona

[edit]

The corona is the Sun's outer atmosphere, a thin plasma of over a million kelvin that can be seen during a total eclipse.

The corona is made of very hot, thin gas that streams out into space as the solar wind.

Life cycle

[edit]

The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago and is about halfway through its life on the main sequence.

In about five billion years it will swell into a red giant and later shrink into a white dwarf.

Observation and safety

[edit]

Looking straight at the Sun, even briefly, can damage the retina; it should be watched only through proper solar filters or by projection.

Malaria

Malaria
SpecialtyInfectious disease
SymptomsFever, vomiting, headache, yellow skin
ComplicationsSeizures, coma, organ failure, anemia
Usual onset10–15 days after exposure
CausesPlasmodium spread by mosquitoes
Diagnostic methodExamination of the blood, antigen detection tests
PreventionMosquito nets, insect repellent, mosquito control, medications
MedicationAntimalarial medication
Frequencyabout 249 million (2022)
Deathsabout 608,000 (2022)

Malaria is a disease spread by mosquitoes that affects humans and other animals.[35] It is caused by single-celled parasites of the genus Plasmodium, passed on by the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito.

Symptoms usually begin ten to fifteen days after the bite and include fever, tiredness, vomiting and headache. In severe cases it can cause yellow skin, seizures, coma or death.

Signs and symptoms

[edit]

The first symptoms are often like those of influenza: fever, chills, headache, muscle aches and tiredness.[36] A classic sign is a cycle of sudden coldness followed by shivering and then fever and sweating, every two or three days.

Complications

[edit]

Severe malaria is usually caused by Plasmodium falciparum. It can lead to breathing problems, low blood sugar, kidney failure and swelling of the brain, called cerebral malaria.

Children under five and pregnant women are at the greatest risk of dying from it.

Recurrence

[edit]

P. vivax and P. ovale can lie dormant in the liver and cause new attacks months or years later. A separate medicine, primaquine or tafenoquine, is needed to clear the liver stage.

Cause

[edit]

Five species of Plasmodium infect humans; P. falciparum causes most deaths, while P. vivax is the most widespread outside Africa.

Transmission

[edit]

Only female Anopheles mosquitoes spread malaria, and most bite between dusk and dawn.[37] It can also pass through blood transfusions and from mother to baby, but not from person to person by touch.

Life cycle

[edit]

The parasites travel in the blood to the liver, where they multiply, and then burst out to infect red blood cells.

When another mosquito bites an infected person, it takes up parasites and the cycle goes on.

Diagnosis

[edit]

Malaria is usually confirmed by looking at a drop of blood under a microscope, stained to show the parasites, or with a rapid antigen test.[38]

Rapid tests

[edit]

Rapid diagnostic tests give a result from a finger-prick of blood in about fifteen minutes and need no laboratory, which makes them useful in remote places.

Prevention

[edit]

Malaria can be prevented by avoiding mosquito bites and by taking medicines.[39]

Mosquito control

[edit]

Sleeping under a bed net treated with insecticide lowers the risk of infection and of death among children by about a fifth.

Spraying the inside walls of houses with insecticide and draining standing water also reduce the number of mosquitoes.

Medications

[edit]

Travellers to areas where malaria is common are advised to take preventive medicines; which one depends on the area and on the person, and should be chosen with a health worker.

No preventive medicine is fully effective, so bite prevention is still needed.

Vaccine

[edit]

Two vaccines, RTS,S and R21, were recommended by the World Health Organization in 2021 and 2023 for children in areas with moderate to high transmission.

Treatment

[edit]

Malaria is treated with antimalarial medicines; the choice depends on the species, how severe the illness is and where it was caught.[40]

Uncomplicated malaria

[edit]

Uncomplicated falciparum malaria is treated with artemisinin-based combination therapy, which pairs an artemisinin with a second medicine that lasts longer in the body.

Severe malaria

[edit]

Severe malaria is a medical emergency. It is treated in hospital with artesunate given into a vein or muscle, followed by a full course of combination therapy.

Anyone with fever after being in a malaria area should seek medical care the same day.

Resistance

[edit]

Parasites resistant to chloroquine are now found in most areas, and resistance to artemisinin has appeared in South-east Asia and parts of East Africa.

Epidemiology

[edit]

About 249 million cases and 608,000 deaths were estimated in 2022, about 95 percent of them in Africa.[41]

History

[edit]

The name comes from the medieval Italian mala aria, bad air, because the disease was blamed on the air of marshes.

Charles Laveran found the parasite in the blood of a patient in 1880, and Ronald Ross showed in 1897 that mosquitoes carry it.

Society and culture

[edit]

Malaria costs Africa billions of dollars a year in health care and lost work, and it keeps many children out of school.

Snakebite

Snakebite
SpecialtyEmergency medicine, toxicology
SymptomsTwo puncture wounds, redness, swelling, severe pain
TreatmentKeeping the bitten person calm, antivenom
Deathsabout 81,000 to 138,000 a year

A snakebite is an injury caused by the bite of a snake, especially one that injects venom.[42] A common sign of a bite from a venomous snake is two puncture wounds from its fangs.

Many bites, even from venomous snakes, inject little or no venom; but every bite should be treated as dangerous until a trained person has seen it.

Signs and symptoms

[edit]

Bites from vipers often cause pain, swelling and bruising that spread up the limb, and bleeding from the gums.

Bites from cobras, kraits and mambas may cause little pain but drooping eyelids, trouble swallowing and weakness that can stop breathing.

Complications

[edit]

Venom can cause kidney failure, death of tissue around the bite and loss of the limb.

Prevention

[edit]

Wear boots and long trousers in the bush, use a torch at night and do not put hands into holes or under rocks.

Do not try to catch or kill a snake; many bites happen that way.

First aid

[edit]

Move away from the snake and keep the bitten person as calm and still as possible; moving spreads the venom faster.[43]

Remove rings, watches and tight clothing near the bite before swelling starts.

Keep the bitten limb still, for example with a splint, at about the level of the heart.

Get the person to a hospital that has antivenom as quickly as possible.

What not to do

[edit]

Do not cut the wound, suck out the venom, apply a tight tourniquet, apply ice or give alcohol; these do not help and can do harm.

Do not wait for symptoms to appear before going to hospital.

Treatment

[edit]

Antivenom is the only specific treatment for venomous snakebite, and it should be given in hospital by trained staff because it can cause severe allergic reactions.[44]

Antivenom

[edit]

An antivenom works only against the venom of certain snakes, so it helps to know or describe the snake, but a photo taken from a safe distance is enough; never try to catch it.

Supportive care

[edit]

People with paralysis may need a machine to help them breathe, and people with kidney failure may need dialysis.

Epidemiology

[edit]

About 5.4 million people are bitten each year, and most deaths happen in South Asia and Africa among farmers and children.

Kidney stone disease

Kidney stone disease is when a solid piece of material, a kidney stone, forms in the urinary tract.[45] Small stones may pass without symptoms; a stone larger than about 5 mm can block the ureter and cause severe pain.

About one in ten people have a kidney stone at some time in their life.

Signs and symptoms

[edit]

The typical symptom is severe pain in the lower back or side that comes in waves and may spread to the groin, often with nausea, vomiting and blood in the urine.

Causes

[edit]

Not drinking enough water is the main risk; obesity, some foods and some medicines also raise it.

Composition

[edit]

About 80 percent of kidney stones are calcium stones, mostly calcium oxalate and some calcium phosphate.[46]

Uric acid stones form in acid urine, often in people with gout.

Struvite stones, made of magnesium ammonium phosphate, grow after infections with certain bacteria and can fill the kidney.

Cystine stones are rare and run in families.

Diagnosis

[edit]

A CT scan without contrast finds almost all stones; ultrasound is used in pregnancy and in children.

Prevention

[edit]

Drinking enough fluid to pass more than two litres of urine a day prevents most new stones.[47]

Eating less salt and less animal protein helps; cutting calcium from the diet does not, and may raise the risk.

Treatment

[edit]

Pain is treated with anti-inflammatory medicines; most stones under 5 mm pass by themselves within weeks.

Larger stones can be broken with shock waves from outside the body or removed through a thin tube.

A blocked kidney with fever is an emergency and needs care the same day.

pages.wikivoyage_en_all_maxi_2026-02/Mombasa:
Mombasa

Mombasa is Kenya's second city and its main port, on an island in the Indian Ocean joined to the mainland by bridges, a causeway and a ferry. It is hot, humid and busy, with an old Swahili town, a Portuguese fort and beaches to the north and south.

Most visitors pass through on their way to the beach resorts, but the old town repays a day or two of walking.

Understand

[edit]

Mombasa has been a trading town for at least a thousand years, and its people are a mix of Swahili, Arab, Indian and up-country Kenyan families. Swahili is spoken everywhere; English is widely understood in hotels and shops.

History

[edit]

The Portuguese built Fort Jesus in 1593 to control the coast, and the town changed hands several times between the Portuguese and the Omani Arabs.

The British made Mombasa the start of the Uganda Railway in 1896, and the port grew into the largest in East Africa.

Climate

[edit]

It is hot all year, with daytime highs around 30 °C. The long rains fall from April to June and the short rains in November; January to March is hottest and driest.

Get in

[edit]

By plane

[edit]

Moi International Airport (MBA) is on the mainland about 10 km west of the island, with flights from Nairobi taking about an hour and some direct charter flights from Europe.

A taxi from the airport to the island costs around KSh 1,500 to 2,000; agree the fare before you get in. Matatus pass on the main road outside the airport gate.

By train

[edit]

The Madaraka Express runs from Nairobi to the Mombasa terminus at Miritini, on the mainland, in about five to six hours. Tickets sell out on weekends and holidays, so book a few days ahead.

From Miritini station a shuttle bus and taxis run to the island, a 30-minute ride without traffic.

By bus

[edit]

Many companies run day and night buses from Nairobi, taking eight to ten hours. They arrive near the Mwembe Tayari area of the island.

By boat

[edit]

Dhows and small cargo boats sail to Zanzibar and Lamu, but there are no regular passenger services and safety standards are low.

Get around

[edit]

The island is small enough to walk across in an hour, but the heat makes short rides welcome. Traffic on the bridges and at the ferry is heavy at rush hour.

By matatu

[edit]

Matatus, shared minibuses, run on fixed routes across the island and to the north and south coasts. A ride within the island costs KSh 50 to 100; pay the conductor in cash.

They are cheap but crowded, and drivers are known for reckless overtaking.

By tuk-tuk

[edit]

Tuk-tuks, three-wheeled motor taxis, are everywhere and take up to three passengers. A short ride in town is around KSh 150 to 300; agree the price first, or use a ride-hailing app.

By boda-boda

[edit]

Motorbike taxis are the fastest way through traffic but have many accidents. Insist on a helmet or take something else.

By ferry

[edit]

The Likoni ferry links the island to the south coast and is free for foot passengers. It is very crowded at rush hour, and pickpockets work the queues.

See

[edit]
  •  Fort Jesus, Nkrumah Rd, at the end of the old town. daily 08:00-18:00. Non-residents KSh 1,200. The Portuguese fort, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and museum, with thick coral walls, cannons and a small collection of finds from shipwrecks. Allow two hours.
  •  Old Town. Narrow streets of carved wooden doors and balconies, small mosques and spice shops, best walked in the cooler morning. Hire a licensed guide at the fort gate for a short tour.
  •  Tusks. Two pairs of crossed aluminium tusks over Moi Avenue, put up for a royal visit in 1952 and now the city's symbol.
  •  Haller Park, Bamburi, 10 km north. daily 08:00-17:00. A former limestone quarry turned into a nature park, with giraffes, hippos, tortoises and a crocodile pond.

Do

[edit]

Swim and sunbathe at the beaches of Nyali and Bamburi to the north, or Diani, 30 km to the south. The water is calm inside the reef at high tide.

Snorkel or dive at the Mombasa Marine National Park, where boats take you out to coral gardens off Nyali. Pay the park fee at the Kenya Wildlife Service office.

  •  Dhow dinner cruise. about US$70 per person. An evening sail around the island in a traditional dhow with dinner and music, leaving from the old port.

Watch a football match of the local club, Bandari, at the municipal stadium.

Buy

[edit]

The currency is the Kenyan shilling (KSh). ATMs are common on Moi Avenue and Nkrumah Road and in the malls; most accept foreign Visa and Mastercard cards.

M-Pesa, the mobile money system, is used for almost everything, even by street sellers. Visitors can register a local SIM card for it with a passport.

Bargain hard in the markets; a fair price is often half of the first one asked.

  •  Biashara Street, Biashara St, old town. Rows of shops selling kikoi and kanga cloth, the bright wraps worn on the coast.
  •  Marikiti Market. The main fruit and vegetable market, loud and colourful, with spice stalls on its edge.

Eat

[edit]

Coastal food is rich in coconut, rice, fish and spices. Try biryani, pilau, samaki wa kupaka (grilled fish in coconut sauce), and street snacks of cassava crisps and mahamri, a doughnut made with coconut milk.

Budget

[edit]
  •  Sultan Kitchen, Digo Rd. KSh 300-600. Busy canteen with cheap biryani and fresh juices, run by the same family for forty years.
  •  Mama Fatuma's. KSh 200-500. Street-side stall with grilled fish and chapati in the evening near the old port.

Mid-range

[edit]
  •  Blue Room Grill, Haile Selassie Rd. KSh 600-1,500. Long-running place for Indian snacks, burgers and ice cream, with air conditioning.

Splurge

[edit]
  •  Coral Terrace, Mama Ngina Dr. KSh 3,000 and up. Seafood on a terrace over the creek, with crab and lobster by weight. Book for sunset.

Drink

[edit]

Mombasa is a largely Muslim city, and the old town has few bars, but beer is easy to find in hotels and in Nyali.

Tap water is not safe to drink; buy bottled water or use a filter.

  •  Tamarind Bar, Nyali. 16:00-late. Cocktails over the water with live music at weekends.

Sleep

[edit]

Budget

[edit]
  •  Lotus Guest House. doubles from KSh 3,000. Simple, clean rooms with fans in an old building near the fort, good for backpackers.

Mid-range

[edit]
  •  Castle View Hotel. doubles from KSh 8,000. Air-conditioned rooms in the town centre, with a rooftop restaurant.

Splurge

[edit]
  •  Nyali Shore Resort. from US$200. Large beach hotel with pools and its own reef, 15 minutes north of the island.

Stay safe

[edit]

Mombasa is safer than Nairobi, but petty theft is common. Do not walk alone on empty beaches or in the old town after dark, and take a taxi at night.

Beach boys selling tours and souvenirs can be pushy; a firm no thank you usually works.

Swim only where others are swimming: currents are strong at the reef gaps, and sea urchins live on the reef flats.

Police roadblocks are common; carry a copy of your passport.

In an emergency dial 999 or 112 from any phone.

Stay healthy

[edit]

Malaria is present on the coast all year. Take anti-malarial tablets as advised by a doctor, sleep under a net and use repellent in the evening.

Dengue fever also occurs, spread by mosquitoes that bite in the day.

Drink plenty of water and stay out of the midday sun; heat exhaustion is a real risk.

  •  Coast General Hospital, Moi Ave. The main public hospital, busy but with an emergency department.
  •  Mombasa Hospital, Mama Ngina Dr, ☏ +254 41 2312191. Private hospital preferred by visitors, with good emergency care.

Connect

[edit]

Mobile coverage is good, and a local SIM card with data is cheap. Most hotels and cafes have free wifi.

Go next

[edit]

Diani Beach, an hour south across the Likoni ferry, has a long white beach and many resorts.

Malindi and Watamu, two to three hours north, have more beaches and the ruins of Gedi.

Tsavo East National Park is about two hours inland, for a short safari.
pages.wikivoyage_en_all_maxi_2026-02/Cusco:
Cusco

Cusco is a city in the Andes of southern Peru, the old capital of the Inca Empire and the gateway to Machu Picchu. It stands at about 3,400 m above sea level, and many visitors feel the altitude on their first days.

Its centre mixes Inca stone walls with Spanish churches and colonial mansions, and it is one of the most visited cities in South America.

Understand

[edit]

The Inca rebuilt Cusco in the fifteenth century, and the Spanish built their churches on the Inca foundations after 1534.

Spanish is the main language, and Quechua is spoken by many people in the villages around the city.

Climate

[edit]

The dry season, May to September, has clear sunny days and very cold nights, sometimes below freezing. The wet season runs from November to March.

Get in

[edit]

By plane

[edit]

Alejandro Velasco Astete airport (CUZ) is 5 km from the centre and has many daily flights from Lima, taking about 75 minutes.

Taxis from the airport to the Plaza de Armas cost about 25 soles; official taxis wait inside the arrivals hall.

By bus

[edit]

Buses from Lima take about 22 hours, and from Puno on Lake Titicaca about seven hours. The main bus terminal is south of the centre.

Get around

[edit]

The historic centre is compact and best seen on foot, but the streets are steep and the air is thin, so walk slowly.

Taxis are cheap; a ride within the centre should cost 5 to 10 soles. Use taxis called by your hotel at night.

Colectivos, shared minivans, leave for the Sacred Valley from Calle Pavón.

See

[edit]
  •  Plaza de Armas. The main square, once the heart of the Inca city, with the cathedral and the Compañía church on two sides.
  •  Qorikancha. 15 soles. The Inca Temple of the Sun, whose walls were covered in gold; a Dominican convent stands on top of it.
  •  Sacsayhuamán. daily 07:00-17:30. Huge zigzag walls of fitted stones on the hill above the city, a steep 30-minute walk up.

Many sights need the boleto turístico, a combined ticket for 16 sites valid for ten days, which costs 130 soles.

Do

[edit]

Walk to Machu Picchu on the Inca Trail, a four-day hike that must be booked months ahead with a licensed agency.

Visit the markets and ruins of the Sacred Valley, at Pisac and Ollantaytambo, on a day trip.

Take a Spanish course; many schools offer a week of lessons with a homestay.

Buy

[edit]

The currency is the Peruvian sol. ATMs are plentiful around the Plaza de Armas, but they charge a fee and some limit each withdrawal.

Many small shops and markets take only cash, and US dollars in good condition can be changed at casas de cambio on Avenida El Sol.

Alpaca wool sweaters and blankets are sold everywhere; real baby alpaca is soft and costs more.

Eat

[edit]

Try cuy (roast guinea pig), alpaca steak, rocoto relleno and the many potato dishes of the Andes.

  •  Mercado San Pedro. 06:00-18:00. The central market, with stalls selling soups, juices and set lunches for a few soles.
  •  Inka Grill. mains 40-70 soles. Andean dishes in a polished dining room on the main square.

Drink

[edit]

Coca tea, made from coca leaves steeped in hot water, is served everywhere and helps many people with the altitude.

Pisco sour is the national cocktail. Nightclubs around the Plaza de Armas stay open until the early morning.

Sleep

[edit]

Cusco has hundreds of hostels and hotels. Rooms on hills above the plaza can mean a hard climb at altitude; some hotels pump oxygen into rooms.

  •  Casa Andina Wasi. doubles from 150 soles. Quiet guest house in a colonial courtyard five minutes from the plaza.

Stay safe

[edit]

Cusco is fairly safe, but pickpockets work in the markets and at the bus terminal. Keep bags in front of you in crowds.

Use only registered taxis, especially at night, and do not accept drinks from strangers in bars.

Protests and road blockades happen from time to time and can close the railway to Machu Picchu.

Stay healthy

[edit]

Altitude sickness is the main health risk. Rest on your first day, drink plenty of water, avoid alcohol and climb slowly.[48]

Headache, nausea and breathlessness are common at first; if symptoms get worse, go down to a lower altitude and see a doctor.

Many visitors sleep their first nights in the Sacred Valley, about 600 m lower, and visit the city later.

The tap water is not safe to drink; use bottled or boiled water.

The sun is fierce at this height; use sunscreen and a hat even when it is cold.

Go next

[edit]

Machu Picchu is reached by train from Ollantaytambo or Poroy to Aguas Calientes, then by bus up the mountain.

Puno and Lake Titicaca are a day's bus or train ride to the south-east.
pages.wikivoyage_en_all_maxi_2026-02/Lisbon:
Lisbon

Lisbon is the capital of Portugal, spread over seven hills above the wide mouth of the Tagus river. Its old quarters of steep lanes, tiled facades and yellow trams make it one of the most attractive cities in Europe.

It is mild all year, and the beaches of Cascais and Costa da Caparica are within an hour.

Understand

A great earthquake in 1755, followed by fire and a tsunami, destroyed most of the city; the grid of the Baixa was built afterwards.

Portuguese is the language; many people in the centre speak English, and Spanish is widely understood.

Districts

Alfama, the oldest quarter, climbs the hill below the castle. Bairro Alto is quiet by day and full of bars at night. Belém, to the west, has the great monuments of the age of discovery.

Get in

By plane

Humberto Delgado Airport (LIS) is only 7 km north of the centre. The red metro line runs from the airport to the city in about 20 minutes for under €2.

Taxis from the airport cost about €15 to €20 to the centre; ride-hailing apps are often cheaper.

By train

Fast trains from Porto arrive at Santa Apolónia and Oriente stations, taking about three hours. There is a night train from Spain on some routes.

Get around

By public transport

A rechargeable Viva Viagem card works on the metro, buses, trams, funiculars and ferries; a 24-hour pass costs about €7.

The metro has four lines and runs from 06:30 to 01:00.

By tram

Tram 28 rattles through Graça, Alfama, Baixa and Estrela, and it is the easiest way to see the old quarters, but it is packed in summer.

Pickpockets are very active on tram 28; keep your bag closed and in front of you.

On foot

Walking is the best way to see the centre, but the hills are steep and the polished stone pavements are slippery when wet. Wear shoes with good grip.

See

  •  Castelo de São Jorge. 09:00-21:00 (to 18:00 in winter). €15. Moorish castle on the highest hill, with views over the city and the river.
  •  Jerónimos Monastery, Belém. €12. A vast monastery in the Manueline style, paid for with the wealth of the spice trade; Vasco da Gama is buried here.
  •  Belém Tower. Small fortress on the river from which ships set out for India and Brazil.

Do

Listen to fado, the melancholy songs of Lisbon, in a small restaurant in Alfama or Mouraria.

Take the ferry across the river to Cacilhas for the view back to the city and grilled fish by the water.

Spend a day at the beach in Cascais, 40 minutes by train from Cais do Sodré.

Buy

Portugal uses the euro. Cards are widely accepted, but small cafes and kiosks may want cash for small amounts.

Tipping is not expected; rounding up the bill or leaving 5 to 10 percent in a restaurant is generous.

Look for canned sardines in decorated tins, cork goods and painted tiles.

Eat

Lisbon is known for grilled sardines in June, salt cod (bacalhau) in many forms, and pastéis de nata, custard tarts with flaky pastry.

Bread, olives and cheese put on the table before the meal are not free; you pay for what you eat.

  •  Cervejaria do Cais. €25-40. Busy seafood hall with prawns and crab by the kilo.

Drink

Bairro Alto and Cais do Sodré are the centres of nightlife, where crowds drink in the streets until late.

Ginjinha, a sour cherry liqueur, is served in tiny glasses at stand-up bars near Rossio.

Sleep

Book well ahead in summer. Baixa and Chiado are central and flat; Alfama is charming but hilly.

  •  Rio Hostel. dorm beds from €25. Friendly hostel in a renovated building near the river, with dorms and private rooms.

Stay safe

Lisbon is one of the safest capitals in Europe, but pickpockets work the trams, the Baixa and the viewpoints.

In Baixa and Bairro Alto, men may quietly offer drugs; they are usually selling crushed bay leaves or flour, and buying anything is illegal.

The European emergency number 112 works everywhere.

Connect

Free wifi is common in cafes and in some squares. EU mobile users pay home rates.

Go next

Sintra, 40 minutes by train, has palaces and gardens in wooded hills.

Évora, two hours east, is a walled town with a Roman temple.
pages.wikivoyage_en_all_maxi_2026-02/Kampala:
Kampala

Kampala is the capital and largest city of Uganda, spread over a series of green hills near the northern shore of Lake Victoria. It is a lively, friendly and chaotic city of about 1.7 million people, with many more in its suburbs.

Most visitors use Kampala as a base for trips to the source of the Nile at Jinja, the gorillas of the south-west and the national parks.

Understand

[edit]

Kampala grew around the palace of the Kabaka, the king of Buganda, on Mengo hill, and the British fort on Old Kampala hill. Each of its hills still has its own character: Kololo for embassies, Namirembe and Rubaga for cathedrals, Kibuli for the mosque.

English and Luganda are spoken everywhere; Swahili is also understood.

Climate

[edit]

Kampala is close to the equator but high, at about 1,200 m, so it is warm rather than hot, with highs around 27 °C all year. Rain falls in two seasons, March to May and September to November, usually as short heavy storms in the afternoon.

Get in

[edit]

By plane

[edit]

Entebbe International Airport (EBB) is 40 km south of Kampala on the shore of the lake. Flights come from Nairobi, Addis Ababa, Doha, Dubai, Istanbul, Amsterdam and Brussels.

The Entebbe Expressway makes the drive to the city about 45 minutes, but traffic in the city itself can double that.

A private taxi to central Kampala costs about USh 100,000 to 150,000; agree the price before leaving. Shared minibuses run from Entebbe town to the old taxi park for a few thousand shillings.

By bus

[edit]

Overnight buses link Kampala with Nairobi in 12 to 14 hours, and with Kigali in about 10 hours. Book with a well-known company and ask which border post the bus crosses.

Get around

[edit]

Traffic is heavy from 07:00 to 10:00 and from 16:00 to 20:00, and the roads are steep and potholed. Allow plenty of time for any journey across the city.

By minibus taxi

[edit]

White and blue minibuses, called taxis, leave from the old and new taxi parks in the centre for every part of the city. They leave when full and stop anywhere on request; a fare within the city is USh 1,000 to 3,000.

The taxi parks are crowded and confusing; ask a conductor for the right vehicle and watch your pockets.

By boda-boda

[edit]

Motorbike taxis, boda-bodas, are everywhere and are the fastest way through traffic. They are also the cause of many serious injuries and deaths; hospital wards in Kampala are full of boda-boda crash victims.

If you must use one, wear a helmet, tell the driver to go slowly and use a ride-hailing app, which records the trip.

By special hire

[edit]

Special hire cars are private taxis, usually old saloon cars, found at stands near hotels and markets. Ride-hailing apps work in Kampala and are often cheaper and easier than bargaining.

See

[edit]
  •  Kasubi Tombs, Kasubi hill. daily 08:00-18:00. USh 10,000. Burial place of four kings of Buganda in a great thatched hut, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The main tomb burnt in 2010 and has been rebuilt by traditional methods.
  •  Uganda Museum, Kira Rd, Kamwokya. daily 10:00-18:00. The oldest museum in East Africa, with a good collection of traditional musical instruments that visitors can play.
  •  Gaddafi National Mosque. outside prayer times. Large white mosque on Old Kampala hill; climb the minaret for the best view over the city. Women are lent a headscarf and wrap at the entrance.
  •  Namirembe Cathedral. Anglican cathedral on the hill of the same name, with a wide view from its grounds.

Do

[edit]

Watch a performance of traditional dance and drumming at the Ndere Centre on a Sunday, Wednesday or Friday evening.

Take a boat trip on Lake Victoria from Munyonyo or Ggaba to see birds and fishing villages.

Go rafting on the Nile at Jinja, two hours east, where companies run day trips from Kampala with pick-up at hotels.

  •  Owino Market walk. A guided walk through St Balikuddembe Market, the biggest in East Africa, where everything from second-hand clothes to spices is sold.

Buy

[edit]

The currency is the Ugandan shilling (USh). US dollar notes printed before 2006 are not accepted, and small notes get a worse rate.

Forex bureaus in the centre and in the malls give better rates than banks. ATMs are common; Stanbic and Absa machines take foreign Visa cards.

Mobile money (MTN MoMo and Airtel Money) is used to pay for almost everything, including taxis and market stalls.

  •  Exposure Africa, Buganda Rd. Craft village of about thirty small shops selling baskets, bark cloth, drums and carvings; bargain politely.

Eat

[edit]

The staple is matoke, steamed and mashed green bananas, served with groundnut sauce, beans or meat stew.

The famous street snack is the rolex, an omelette with cabbage and tomato rolled in a chapati, sold for about USh 2,000.

  •  Mama Ruth's Kitchen, Kampala Rd. USh 10,000-15,000. Local buffet of matoke, posho, beans, greens and stews; you pay by the plate.
  •  Lakeview Terrace. USh 30,000-60,000. Fish from the lake, grilled whole, with a view over the water at Ggaba.

Drink

[edit]

Kampala's nightlife is famous in East Africa, with bars and clubs open until dawn in Kabalagala, Bugolobi and Kololo.

Local beers are Nile Special and Club; waragi is a strong local gin.

  •  Hilltop Lounge, Kololo. Rooftop bar with live music on Fridays and a view of the city lights.

Sleep

[edit]

Budget

[edit]
  •  Red Chilli Hideaway. dorm beds from USh 40,000. Long-running backpackers' place in a quiet compound in Bukoto, with dorms, camping and a restaurant; it also runs trips to the parks.

Mid-range

[edit]
  •  Hill View Guest House. doubles from US$60. Clean rooms with hot water and breakfast, near the centre but out of the noise.

Splurge

[edit]
  •  Lakeside Grand. from US$220. Large hotel with a pool and gardens on Nakasero hill, popular with business travellers.

Stay safe

[edit]

Kampala is fairly safe by the standards of African capitals, but bag snatching and pickpocketing are common, especially in the taxi parks, Owino Market and on Kampala Road after dark.

Do not walk alone at night; take a special hire or an app taxi.

Boda-boda crashes are the biggest danger to visitors; see Get around.

Demonstrations sometimes turn violent; avoid crowds and follow local news.

Homosexual acts are illegal in Uganda and punished severely; same-sex couples should be very discreet.

Stay healthy

[edit]

Malaria is present; take anti-malarial medicine on a doctor's advice and use a mosquito net.

Do not swim in Lake Victoria near the shore: the water carries bilharzia, a parasite that enters through the skin.

Tap water is not safe to drink; bottled water is sold everywhere.

  •  Nsambya Hospital, Nsambya hill. Large private mission hospital with a 24-hour emergency department.
  •  International Hospital Kampala, Namuwongo, ☏ +256 312 200400. Private hospital used by most visitors and expatriates, with good emergency care.

Connect

[edit]

MTN and Airtel sell SIM cards at the airport and in shops; you need your passport to register one.

Go next

[edit]

Jinja, two hours east, for the Nile, rafting and kayaking.

Entebbe, for the botanical gardens and the wildlife centre, on the way to the airport.

Murchison Falls National Park, five hours north, for the falls and boat trips among hippos and crocodiles.
pages.wikivoyage_en_all_maxi_2026-02/Serengeti:
Serengeti National Park

Serengeti National Park is a vast park of grassland and savanna in northern Tanzania, famous for the great migration of over a million wildebeest and hundreds of thousands of zebras, followed by lions, cheetahs and hyenas.

It covers about 14,750 km² and borders the Maasai Mara of Kenya to the north.

Understand

The migration moves in a yearly circle: the herds give birth in the southern plains from January to March, move west and north from May, cross the Mara River from July to October and return south with the short rains in November.

Fees and permits

Park fees are paid by card at the gates; cash is not accepted. The fee for a foreign adult is about US$70 to 80 per day plus VAT, and every night in the park needs a fee.

Fees must be paid for each 24-hour period, so entering in the afternoon and leaving before the same time next day counts as one day.

Get in

Most visitors arrive on an organised safari from Arusha, about eight hours by road through the Ngorongoro Conservation Area.

Small planes fly from Arusha to airstrips at Seronera, Kogatende and other camps in about one to two hours.

Get around

Visitors must stay in vehicles except at marked places, and driving off the tracks is forbidden in most of the park.

Driving is allowed only from 06:00 to 18:00; vehicles out after dark are fined.

The roads are rough gravel and become slippery in the rains; a four-wheel-drive vehicle with a pop-up roof is best.

See

Seronera, in the centre, has lions and leopards all year, and the best chance of seeing big cats.

The Mara River crossings in the north, from July to October, are the most dramatic sight of the migration, when crocodiles wait for the herds.

Kopjes, rocky outcrops in the plains, are a favourite place of lions.

Do

Take a hot-air balloon flight at dawn over the plains, followed by breakfast in the bush; flights cost about US$600 per person.

Walking safaris with an armed ranger are possible in some areas; book through your operator.

Sleep

Lodges and tented camps range from simple public campsites to luxury camps that move with the migration.

  •  Seronera public campsite. US$30 per person plus fees. Basic campsite with toilets and a cooking shelter; hyenas walk through at night, so keep food in the vehicle.

Stay safe

The animals are wild and dangerous. Never leave your vehicle except where allowed, and never get between a mother and her young.

At campsites, do not walk around after dark without a ranger, and never leave food in your tent.

Tsetse flies, which bite painfully, are attracted to dark blue and black clothing; wear light colours.

Stay healthy

Malaria is present in the park; take preventive medicine on advice and cover up at dusk.

Bring enough drinking water for long drives, as the park is hot and dusty and lodges are far apart.

Go next

Ngorongoro Crater, on the way back to Arusha, has dense wildlife in a volcanic caldera.

Lake Natron, to the north-east, has flamingos and the active volcano Ol Doinyo Lengai.
pages.wikivoyage_en_all_maxi_2026-02/Inca_Trai:
Inca Trail

The Inca Trail is a four-day hike of about 42 km through the Andes of Peru to the ruins of Machu Picchu, along a stone path built by the Inca. It crosses three passes, the highest at 4,215 m.

Understand

[edit]

Only 500 people a day, including guides and porters, may start the trail, and every hiker must go with a licensed operator. The trail is closed every February for maintenance.

Prepare

[edit]

Permits sell out months ahead for May to August; book four to six months in advance. Your passport number is on the permit and must match the passport you carry.

Spend at least two days in Cusco or the Sacred Valley before starting, to get used to the altitude.

Bring rain gear, warm layers for nights below freezing, broken-in boots and a headlamp.

Get in

[edit]

Operators drive hikers from Cusco to the start at kilometre 82 near Ollantaytambo, about two hours away.

Go

[edit]

Day 1

[edit]

The first day is gentle, about 12 km along the Urubamba valley past the ruins of Llactapata to camp at Wayllabamba.

Day 2

[edit]

The hardest day climbs about 1,200 m to Dead Woman's Pass at 4,215 m and drops steeply to camp at Pacaymayo. Go slowly and drink plenty of water.

Day 3

[edit]

The longest day crosses two more passes and passes the finest ruins of the trail, Runkurakay, Sayacmarca and Wiñay Wayna.

Day 4

[edit]

Hikers wake at about 03:30 to reach the Sun Gate, Inti Punku, at dawn and walk down into Machu Picchu.

Stay safe

[edit]

Altitude sickness is the main danger; if a hiker has a severe headache, confusion or breathlessness at rest, they must go down, and guides carry oxygen.

The stone steps are steep and slippery in the rain; use walking poles with rubber tips, which are required on the trail.

Go next

[edit]

From Machu Picchu, buses go down to Aguas Calientes, where trains leave for Ollantaytambo and Cusco.
pages.wikivoyage_en_all_maxi_2026-02/Altitude_:
Altitude sickness

Altitude sickness, or acute mountain sickness, can affect anyone who goes quickly above about 2,500 m. It is caused by the lower pressure of oxygen at height, and it can kill if it is ignored.

Understand

[edit]

How fit you are does not protect you; young, fit people often climb too fast and suffer more.

Most people adjust within a few days if they climb slowly.

Symptoms

[edit]

The first signs are headache, loss of appetite, nausea, tiredness and poor sleep, usually 6 to 12 hours after arriving at a new height.

Serious forms

[edit]

Fluid on the lungs (HAPE) causes breathlessness at rest, a cough and a gurgling chest. Swelling of the brain (HACE) causes confusion, clumsiness and drowsiness. Both are emergencies.

Prevention

[edit]

Above 3,000 m, do not raise your sleeping height by more than 500 m a night, and rest a day every 3 or 4 days.

Climb high and sleep low: day walks to a higher point help, as long as you come back down to sleep.

Drink enough water, avoid alcohol and sleeping pills, and eat well.

Medication

[edit]

Acetazolamide can help the body adjust and is sometimes taken to prevent altitude sickness; it needs a prescription, and the dose should come from a doctor.

Treatment

[edit]

Never go higher with symptoms. If they do not get better with a day of rest, go down.

With signs of HAPE or HACE, go down at once, even at night, by at least 500 to 1,000 m, and get medical help. Oxygen and a portable pressure bag can save a life while waiting.

Stay safe

[edit]

Do not leave a sick person alone, and do not let them go down alone; confusion can make them wander off.
pages.wikivoyage_en_all_maxi_2026-02/Tanzania:
Tanzania

Tanzania is a country in East Africa, home to Mount Kilimanjaro, the Serengeti, the spice islands of Zanzibar and long beaches on the Indian Ocean. It is one of the best places in Africa for a safari.

Understand

[edit]

Tanzania was formed in 1964 by the union of Tanganyika and Zanzibar. It has been peaceful since independence, and Swahili is spoken by nearly everyone.

The capital is officially Dodoma, but Dar es Salaam is the largest city and the main business centre.

Climate

[edit]

The coast is hot and humid. The long rains fall from March to May and the short rains in November and December; June to October is dry and the best time for safaris.

Regions

[edit]

The northern circuit has the Serengeti, Ngorongoro, Tarangire and Kilimanjaro. The southern parks, such as Nyerere and Ruaha, are wilder and less visited.

Get in

[edit]

Entry requirements

[edit]

Most visitors need a visa, which should be applied for online before travel; a single-entry tourist visa costs about US$50, or US$100 for citizens of the United States.

A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required if you arrive from, or have spent more than 12 hours in transit in, a country with a risk of yellow fever.

By plane

[edit]

The main airports are Julius Nyerere International in Dar es Salaam, Kilimanjaro International between Arusha and Moshi, and Zanzibar.

By land

[edit]

Buses cross from Nairobi to Arusha through the Namanga border in about six hours.

Get around

[edit]

Domestic flights link the main towns and the parks and save long days on bad roads.

Long-distance buses are cheap but some drive dangerously fast; choose a company with a good reputation.

Ferries run from Dar es Salaam to Zanzibar in about two hours.

Talk

[edit]

Swahili is the national language; English is used in business and higher education. A few words of Swahili, such as jambo (hello) and asante (thank you), are much appreciated.

See

[edit]

The great migration in the Serengeti, the crater of Ngorongoro, the old Stone Town of Zanzibar and the snows of Kilimanjaro are the main sights.

Do

[edit]

Climb Kilimanjaro, at 5,895 m the highest mountain in Africa, on a five- to eight-day trek with a licensed guide.

Dive and snorkel off Zanzibar, Pemba and Mafia islands.

Buy

[edit]

The currency is the Tanzanian shilling (TSh). US dollars are widely accepted for park fees, safaris and hotels, but notes older than 2009 are refused.

Tipping safari guides and porters is expected: about US$20 per day per group for a guide is common.

Eat

[edit]

Ugali, a stiff maize porridge, is eaten with stews, beans or greens. On the coast and Zanzibar, food is spicier, with coconut, rice and seafood.

Stay safe

[edit]

Tanzania is generally safe, but bag snatching happens in Dar es Salaam and Arusha, and visitors should avoid walking at night.

Swim only at beaches used by others, and be careful of strong currents on the coast.

Stay healthy

[edit]

Malaria is present across most of the country below 1,800 m; see a doctor about preventive medicine before travelling.

Drink only bottled or treated water.

Altitude sickness is common on Kilimanjaro; climb slowly and go down if symptoms get worse.

Respect

[edit]

Dress modestly in Zanzibar and on the coast, where most people are Muslim: cover shoulders and knees away from the beach.

Always ask before photographing people, especially Maasai.

Written By: Repair Volunteer
  • Comments4

Difficulty

Moderate

Steps

13

Time Required

20 - 40 minutes

Introduction

Use this guide to replace the cooling fan and heat sink of a ThinkPad T480. A noisy or dead fan lets the processor overheat and slow down.

You will need fresh thermal paste, because the old paste is wiped off when the heat sink comes away from the processor.

Tools

  • Phillips #0 Screwdriver

  • Spudger

  • Isopropyl Alcohol

  • Arctic Silver ArctiClean

Parts

  • ThinkPad T480 Fan and Heat Sink

  • Arctic Silver Thermal Paste

  1. Step 1

    • Before you begin, turn off the laptop and unplug the charger.

    • Disable the built-in battery in the BIOS under Config > Power, so the board gets no power while you work.

  2. Step 2

    • Remove the removable rear battery by sliding the two latches toward the centre.

    • Lift the battery out of its bay.

  3. Step 3

    • Loosen the eight captive screws on the bottom cover.

    • The screws stay in the cover, so you do not need to keep track of them.

  4. Step 4

    • Insert a spudger between the bottom cover and the frame near the hinge.

    • Pry along the edge until the clips release.

    • Lift the cover off.

  5. Step 5

    • Disconnect the internal battery cable from the motherboard.

    • Pull the connector straight back by its sides, not by the wires.

  6. Step 6

    • Disconnect the fan cable.

    • It is a small white plug at the left corner of the fan.

  7. Step 7

    • Remove the four Phillips screws that hold the heat sink, in the reverse of the order numbered on it.

    • Work in the order 4, 3, 2, 1 so the heat sink lifts evenly.

    The heat sink screws on mine were captive too, they did not come out at all.

    • Remove the two 5 mm Phillips screws that hold the fan to the frame.

  9. Step 9

    • Lift the fan and heat sink together out of the laptop.

    • If it sticks, twist it gently; the dried paste can hold it to the processor.

  10. Step 10

    • Wipe the old thermal paste off the processor with isopropyl alcohol and a lint-free cloth.

    • Clean the copper plate of the new heat sink the same way.

  11. Step 11

    • Apply a pea-sized drop of thermal paste to the centre of the processor.

    • Do not spread it; the pressure of the heat sink spreads it evenly.
